analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue gun dealers who made illegal sales, without proving fault.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee's crime subcommittee until Congress ended, with no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Anyone shot with a gun that a dealer sold illegally — to a person federal firearms law barred them from selling to — could sue that dealer in federal court for all their injuries, without having to prove the dealer was careless. Victims who won would also get their attorney's fees paid. There were exceptions for people injured while committing a felony and for injuries caused by police or military acting in their duties.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured or who lost family members in shootings involving illegally sold guns. They would gain a new federal right to sue the dealer responsible for the illegal sale, recover direct and consequential damages, and collect attorney's fees if they prevailed. Communities affected by gun violence benefit indirectly if the threat of lawsuits deters dealers from selling to prohibited buyers.

how_it_helps.text: Any person injured or killed by a gun fired after an illegal dealer transfer could sue in any U.S. district court for damages and other relief.

Liability applies without regard to fault or proof of a defect — the victim only has to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the dealer transferred the gun in violation of federal firearms law.
A prevailing plaintiff is awarded reasonable attorney's fees, making it financially possible for individual victims to sue.
The bill adds a remedy without limiting any other cause of action available to shooting victims.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms dealers who make transfers in violation of federal firearms law would owe damages — without regard to fault — for injuries and deaths proximately resulting from the illegal sale, plus plaintiffs' attorney fees. Law-abiding dealers bear essentially no liability because the cause of action is triggered only by an illegal transfer.

drawbacks.text: Strict liability without fault is unusual: once an illegal sale is proven, a dealer owes damages for shootings connected to that sale even though the actual harm was committed by a third person's criminal act — a cost an honest supporter of gun control would still acknowledge.
The bill applies to firearms transferred before enactment and to injuries occurring after enactment, imposing new liability retroactively on past sales.
Consequential damages for all direct and consequential injuries arising from shootings could expose dealers to very large verdicts and liability insurance costs across the retail trade.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: victims of shootings tied to illegal sales get a workable path to compensation, and the fee shifting makes suits financially feasible for ordinary families. The main cost falls on a narrow group — dealers who violate existing federal firearms law — though the strict-liability and retroactive features go beyond what fault-based tort law normally requires, and the potential damages could be very large. On balance, the bill burdens only conduct that is already illegal.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its crime subcommittee, and stayed there until the 103rd Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Jack Reed introduced the Gun Dealer Responsibility Act of 1994 in the House on March 10, 1994, with introductory remarks made the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary on March 10, 1994, and then to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice on March 16, 1994.
No further action was taken: the bill received no cosponsors and died in subcommittee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun dealers who make illegal sales are better off, since they never faced the new liability for injuries caused by their illegal transfers. Firearm retailers generally avoid the prospect of strict-liability damages suits that the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers who make illegal sales

for.name: Rep. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Standing committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice and took no further action — no markup, no report, no floor vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would make dealers who transfer guns illegally strictly liable for injuries and deaths from shootings involving those guns, with plaintiffs' fees added. It targets only illegal sales, so law-abiding dealers lose little, but the industry's interest in shielding itself from gun litigation runs against victims' interest in compensation.
